figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Reverse-engineering individual rules in a complex cognitive domain using programs. (A): Schematic task corpus and associated behavioral data. Each of the four representative ARC tasks $T_{i}$ presents an agent with a small set of input–output training examples from which a hidden transformation rule must be inferred. From a test input, the agent must then construct the corresponding output grid (hidden with a grey square and “?” for illustrative purposes). We use H-ARC, a dataset of responses from over 1,700 participants to the 800 publicly available ARC-AGI-1 tasks. On the right of each task, we show 4 of the most frequent incorrect responses, and the correct response at the bottom. Under each grid, we show the associated response frequency (red for incorrect, green for correct). (B): Behavior-conditioned symbolic synthesis (BCSS). For each unique incorrect response, a large language model is prompted with a full specification of the domain-specific language, task grids, a reference program $P^{*}_{i}$ implementing the target rule for task $T_{i}$, and the observed incorrect response (here, from a human participant). It proposes $k$ independent sets $E_{1},\dots,E_{k}$ of at most $j$ line edits to that program. The schematic edit proposals $E_{l}$ show LLM-sampled proposals which are then applied to $P^{*}_{i}$. Each proposed set of line edits is applied programmatically to the reference program to obtain a new program $E_{l}(P^{*}_{i})$. A custom parser rewrites the programs such that only causally relevant code is retained (i.e., unreferenced lines of code are removed). Each new program $E_{l}(P^{*}_{i})$ is then executed with the test input as argument. Programs whose output reproduces the observed response are kept (green checkmark); all others are discarded (red cross). Because a response is often reachable by more than one unique program, BCSS returns a collection of programs per response rather than a single model. The individual response shown here is also shown surrounded by a red square to the right of task $T_{1}$ in panel A. The constant THREE represents the color green.
figures.headline: Edited reference programs are kept only when they reproduce the observed incorrect response, and all other candidates are discarded.
citing_sentences: The solver must infer the rule and apply it to a new test input by constructing an output grid cell-by-cell (Figure 1A).

The four subsets of participant-level response examples in Figure 1A illustrate that incorrect responses often reflect systematic patterns of inference rather than random or defaulting behavior (incorrect solutions cluster near the correct one shown at the bottom).

As illustrated in Figure 1B, given a reference program $P^{*}_{i}$ implementing the target rule for a task $T_{i}$, an LLM proposes $k$ independent sets of at most $j$ line edits $E_{1},\dots,E_{k}$ to that program.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Synthesized programs suggest people often infer rules simpler than the target rule for a given task. (A): A representative ARC task (94133066). Three training examples demonstrate the target rule—return the contents of the framed sub-grid under whichever of its eight rotations and reflections is consistent with the isolated colored cells scattered around it—followed by the test input for which participants construct an output grid (hidden with a grey square and “?” for illustrative purposes). (B): The reference program $P^{*}$ implementing the target rule for this task. Because this task belongs to the evaluation split, $P^{*}$ is itself model-synthesized rather than human-written. (C): Distribution of relative program length change, $(L(p)-L(P^{*}))/L(P^{*})$, over all synthesized programs, shown separately for the training and evaluation splits of ARC-AGI-1. Treatment programs (blue) are those conditioned on incorrect human responses; control programs (grey) are produced by an identical procedure conditioned instead on the correct output grid. Because edits replace lines in-place and causally irrelevant code is subsequently removed, synthesized programs can either shorten, or remain the same, but never lengthen. Therefore, the control condition controls for the shortening bias attributable to the procedure itself, against which the leftward displacement of the treatment distribution should be read. The dashed line marks the median shortening of modeled responses for the task displayed in this figure. (D): The correct response (top row) and the three of the most frequent incorrect responses to that task, with response frequencies below each grid (green, correct; red, incorrect). For each, we show the diff with $P^{*}$ after applying BCSS, the length of the resulting program relative to $P^{*}$ (blue, retained lines; gray, removed lines; red rule, reference length), which training examples the program reproduces (green, reproduced), and its error category. A single edit can account for a large simplification: for example, replacing the final extract over the eight candidate transforms by one fixed transform renders fourteen lines of the reference program inconsequential, and they are removed. Thus, the simpler resulting program hardcodes a transform instead of exhaustively searching over possible transformations.
figures.headline: Error programs are shorter than reference programs, beyond the shortening seen in control programs built from correct outputs.
citing_sentences: Statistical analyses confirm that DSL programs that capture human responses are credibly simpler than reference programs they are adapted from, on both splits (Figure 2C).

Panel D of Figure 2 illustrate a drastic but intuitive example of simplification: the target rule for this task requires searching over the eight rotations and reflections of a framed sub-grid for the one consistent with the surrounding cells, but the programs reproducing the two bottom responses instead use fixed transforms (hmirror and rot180, respectively), rendering fourteen lines of the reference program irrelevant to the final output.

Every modeled response we display is labeled with its modal error category (panel D, last column of Figures 2–4), illustrating the different ways in which participants can deviate from a single target rule.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Synthesized programs suggest people infer rules that only explain some of the data they observe. (A): A representative ARC task (b230c067). Three training examples specify the target rule—recolor every shape blue except the least common one, which is recolored red—followed by the test input for which participants construct an output grid (hidden with a grey square and “?” for illustrative purposes). (B): A human-written reference program $P^{*}$ implementing the target rule for this task. (C): Top, prevalence of each rule type among all modeled incorrect attempts. A program is a partial-match if it reproduces at least one, but not all, of the training outputs when executed on training inputs; an alternative rule if it reproduces all of them yet still fails the test example; and neither otherwise. Bottom, conditional on an attempt being explained by a partial-match program, the positions of the training examples it reproduces: the first-$k$ or last-$k$ example(s) shown on screen, a contiguous block of at least two examples that doesn’t include the first or last examples, or any other configuration. In both plots, bars give the posterior median attempt-weighted prevalence and error bars the 94% HDI, shown separately for the training (dark) and evaluation (light) splits of ARC-AGI-1; orange dots give the corresponding proportion for the task shown in panel A. (D): The correct response (top row) and three of the most frequent incorrect responses to that task, with response frequencies below each grid (green, correct; red, incorrect). For each, we show the diff with $P^{*}$ after applying BCSS, the length of the resulting program relative to $P^{*}$ (blue, retained lines; gray, removed lines; red rule, reference length), which training examples the program reproduces (green, reproduced), and its error category. The most frequent incorrect response is captured by a program that selects the rightmost object rather than the least common one, a rule that satisfies the first two training examples but not the third.
figures.headline: Many error programs reproduce some training examples but not all, so the inferred rules explain only part of the observed data.
citing_sentences: This subset of programs is split between two rule types: partial-match and alternative rule (Figure 3C, top).

The first incorrect response in Figure 3D illustrates a partial-match rule: the program that captures it selects the rightmost object rather than the least common one, a rule that happens to satisfy the first two training examples but fails on the third.

We labeled each partial-match program by which examples it reproduces: the first or the last $k$ examples shown on screen, a contiguous block of at least two examples, and anything else as “Other” (Figure 3C, bottom).

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Synthesized programs reveal a restricted set of recurring deviations from target rules. (A): A representative ARC task (7fe24cdd). Three training examples specify the target rule—tile the input into a $2\times 2$ arrangement in which each quadrant holds the input rotated by a further 90∘ clockwise, starting from the input at the top left—followed by the test input for which participants construct an output grid (hidden with a gray square and “?” for illustrative purposes). (B): A human-written reference program $P^{*}$ implementing the target rule for this task. (C): Prevalence of each error category among modeled incorrect attempts. An LLM classifier assigned every program one of seven cognitive categories, given the reference program, the task grids, the synthesized program and its execution trace (Table 1 for definitions). Bars give the posterior median of the attempt-weighted prevalence derived from a hierarchical Bayesian categorical model, and error bars the 94% HDI; the categories are mutually exclusive. Classification was performed on programs fitting responses to training split tasks only. (D): The correct response (top row) and three of the most frequent modeled incorrect responses to the task in panel A, with the response frequency below (green, correct; red, incorrect). For each, we show the diff with $P^{*}$ after applying BCSS, the length of the resulting program relative to $P^{*}$ (blue, retained lines; gray, removed lines; red rule, reference length), which training examples the program reproduces when executed on their inputs (green, reproduced), and its error category. The programs that reproduce these three incorrect responses diverge from $P^{*}$ in different ways: omitting the rotations and tiling the input four times, carrying out reflections instead of rotations, or correctly carrying out the rule on a restricted portion of the input.
figures.headline: Modeled errors fall into a restricted set of categories, with attribute misselection largest at 45.2% of attempts.
citing_sentences: Overall, the model finds a dominant category of errors: attribute misselection at 45.2% (94% HDI [43.9, 46.6]) of modeled incorrect attempts (Figure 4C).

Every modeled response we display is labeled with its modal error category (panel D, last column of Figures 2–4), illustrating the different ways in which participants can deviate from a single target rule.
For task 7fe24cdd in Figure 4, the rule is to tile the input into a $2\times 2$ arrangement of successive $90^{\circ}$ rotations.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Machine errors are systematic and performance-dependent. (A): Average accuracy across responses of large reasoning models at different reasoning efforts and humans on the training set of ARC-AGI-1. Note that GPT-OSS-120B uses a mixture-of-experts architecture and thus only has 5.1 billion active parameters during inference. (B): Relative shortening of programs synthesized from model errors compared with programs for correct-output controls; all model configurations exhibit a simplicity bias, which is stronger for lower-performing configurations. (C): The proportion of error programs that partially match or fully reproduce the support examples increases with model performance. (D) Schematic of the classification analysis distinguishing human and machine errors using features derived from synthesized error programs. (E) Within-task ROC-AUC of three fitted classifiers provides evidence of varying degrees of discriminability of human and machine errors on held-out tasks, with less performant models better discriminated from people. Classifiers are trained using linearized program-level feature vectors. ROC-AUC is computed among the errors of each of the 56 shared tasks and averaged across tasks, with error bars showing 95% task-level bootstrap CIs. Panels B and C report results on the subset of 56 tasks where both reasoning language models and people generated incorrect responses (see Appendix S5 for similar trends across all errors). All machine responses are independently sampled, and we restrict comparisons to human first-attempt responses.
figures.headline: Lower-performing models show stronger simplicity bias and are more readily told apart from human errors.
citing_sentences: Figure 5A shows the average accuracy across independent attempts and its standard deviation across runs.
Figure 5B shows the average relative shortening of error programs compared with baseline programs.
Figure 5C shows that the proportion of partial-match rules increases with model capacity, and alternative rules are substantially more frequent for the two highest-performing configurations.

figures.label: Figure S1
figures.caption: Responses within the two-cell noise tolerance. (A–C) Three representative ARC tasks. Left: the training examples and the test input shown to participants (the test output is hidden with a grey square and “?”). Right: for three response grids per task, the output of the best-matching synthesized program (left column) beside the participant responses it is accepted as reproducing (remaining columns); hatched cells indicate that fewer than two distinct responses share that program. The fraction to the left of each row gives the number of participants producing that response out of all participants who attempted the task (red, incorrect; green, correct). Within each row the grids differ in at most two isolated cells (surrounded by white) against the best-match program output.
figures.headline: Responses within the two-cell tolerance differ from the best-matching program output in one or two isolated cells.
citing_sentences: Qualitative analyses revealed that for larger grids, “errors” could often be plausibly attributed to procedural mistakes (i.e., mis-clicks; Supplementary Figure S1).
Supplementary Figure S1 shows representative responses within the tolerance interval.

figures.label: Figure S2
figures.caption: The two-cell cutoff separates procedural noise from rule-level divergence. (A) Coverage of non-trivial incorrect responses as a function of the tolerance $\tau$, attempt-weighted, shown separately for the training (blue) and evaluation (grey) splits. Circles mark the value $\tau=2$ used throughout ($52.5\%$ and $46.2\%$ respectively). (B) Share of mismatched cells that are scattered singletons—no mismatched cell among their four neighbors—as a function of $d$, the mismatch count of the best-scoring candidate program. The steep fall immediately past the cutoff shows that small residuals are isolated misclick-like cells, whereas higher values of $d$ indicate structured regions/objects. (C) Distribution of cell-level distances between incorrect responses and the correct test output, per split. Grey bars ($\leq 2$ mismatched cells) are the near-misses removed by the filter.
figures.headline: Mismatches beyond two cells are rarely isolated single cells, supporting a two-cell cutoff for noise.
citing_sentences: As such, we apply a noise tolerance criterion such that for any “incorrect” response grid of ten or more cells, we filter it out as a “near-miss” if it matches the correct test output grid with up to two mismatched cells; of the $353$ unique near-miss grids we found, $51.3\%$ differed from the correct output by a single cell and $47.9\%$ by exactly two (Supplementary Figure S2, Supplementary Table S1).
Supplementary Figure S2 quantifies the same point over the full dataset.

figures.label: Figure S3
figures.caption: Relative length change as a function of reference complexity and error category. Partial residuals of relative length change against reference-program line count, with the posterior mean slope (dashed) and its 94% HDI (band). Annotations mark the predicted shortening at $L=7$, $14$ and $28$ lines.
figures.headline: Error programs shorten more as reference programs grow longer, by 9.8 percentage points across a four-fold length increase.
citing_sentences: This corresponds to a 9.8 percentage-point difference for a four-fold increase in reference program length (Supplementary Figure S3A).

Supplementary Figure S3 and Supplementary Table S4 report the full output of the program length model of §3.8.4, which regresses relative length change on reference-program line count and task success rate with a soft error-category term.

figures.label: Figure S4
figures.caption: Language models display human-like error category profiles, but order effects are weaker and less consistent than in humans. All panels report values corresponding to the subset of 56 tasks where evaluated LRMs and people both generated at least one incorrect response. Human responses are restricted to first-attempt comparisons. (A) Prevalence of each error category among modeled incorrect machine errors. As with human results, an LLM classifier assigned every program one of seven cognitive categories or unclassifiable, conditioned on the reference program, the task grids, the synthesized program and its execution trace (Table 1 for definitions). Bars give the posterior median of the attempt-weighted prevalence derived from a hierarchical Bayesian categorical model, and error bars the 94% HDI. The categories are mutually exclusive. (B) Conditional on an attempt being explained by a partial-match program, we show the positions of the training examples it reproduces: the first-k or last-k example(s) shown, a contiguous block of at least two examples that does not include the first or last examples, or any other configuration. In both plots, bars give the posterior median attempt-weighted prevalence and error bars the 94% HDI.
figures.headline: Language model error categories resemble human profiles, but order effects are weaker and less consistent than in humans.
citing_sentences: Only GPT-OSS-120B at high reasoning effort shows a human-like order effect, with more first-$k$ than last-$k$ partial matches ($36.1\%$, $94\%$ HDI [$30.8\%,41.4\%$] vs. $21.8\%$ [$16.9\%,26.9\%$]; Supplementary Figure S4B).

The other configurations show no consistent preference for explaining the first examples, with GPT-OSS-120B at medium reasoning effort instead leaning towards last-$k$ matches (Supplementary Figure S4B and Supplementary Table S7).
Lower-performing models instead produce a larger proportion of unclassifiable errors (Supplementary Figure S4A and Supplementary Table S8), suggesting less systematicity.

figures.label: Figure S5
figures.caption: Error-program synthesis prompt (§3.3). The model is given the full DSL specification, the task grids, the reference program implementing the target rule, and the respondent’s incorrect output grid, and returns a structured set of line edits under a fixed JSON schema.
figures.headline: The error-program prompt supplies the full language specification and reference program, and returns line edits in a fixed structured format.
citing_sentences: We sample from the LLM structured outputs of line edits restricted to a JSON schema, and its responses on task grids, a complete DSL reference, the reference program for the in-context task, and an incorrect output grid produced by a human participant or an LLM (Supplementary Figure S5).
Supplementary Figures S5–S8 reproduce the three prompt templates used by the pipeline.

figures.label: Figure S6
figures.caption: Reference-program (solver) synthesis prompt (§3.2.1). Used to generate reference programs for evaluation-split tasks, which have no hand-written solver. The prompt is retrieval-augmented with five solved tasks and their human-written solvers from the training split.
figures.headline: The reference-program prompt includes five retrieved solved tasks to generate solvers for evaluation tasks without hand-written ones.
citing_sentences: To do so, we simply prompted Gemini Pro 3.1 (Supplementary Figure S6) using retrieval-augmented generation (75) with five in-context examples of other tasks and corresponding human-written solvers from the training split.

figures.label: Figure S7
figures.caption: Error-classification prompt (§3.4). The classifier sees the reference program, the task grids, the synthesized error program, and a side-by-side comparison of their behavior on the training examples, and returns one of the seven cognitive categories or the unclassifiable catch-all.
figures.headline: The error-classification prompt compares program and reference behavior on training examples and assigns one of seven categories or unclassifiable.
citing_sentences: Thus, we developed a precise taxonomy of seven error categories which we believed would capture meaningful cognitive constructs, and prompted an LLM (Supplementary Figure S7) to categorize each program from the final filtered collection of programs that match human or machine responses.

figures.label: Figure S8
figures.caption: Evaluation prompt (§3.6). Used to collect machine responses on ARC tasks for comparison with the human data. The model is shown the training pairs and asked to complete the held-out pair.
figures.headline: The evaluation prompt shows training pairs and asks the model to complete the held-out pair for each test input.
citing_sentences: We evaluate each model configuration across ten random seeds using a standard evaluation prompt (see Supplementary Figure S8), on all $416$ test inputs of the $400$ tasks ($4{,}160$ responses per configuration).
Supplementary Figures S5–S8 reproduce the three prompt templates used by the pipeline.

abstract: Symbolic models offer a powerful account of cognition, but their scope has historically been limited by the need for hand-engineering and computational tractability. We show how advances in artificial intelligence (AI) can scale symbolic modeling and help overcome these engineering limitations. We introduce Behavior-Conditioned Symbolic Synthesis (BCSS)—an approach for automated search of interpretable, deterministic symbolic programs that verifiably reproduce behavior—and apply it to model both human and machine behavior across hundreds of challenging reasoning problems. Analyzing these programs reveals that both people and machines tend to oversimplify, adopt rules that are partial explanations for their observations, and misinfer dependencies between problem features. These shared signatures are modulated by available resources, with reasoning effort predicting the extent to which machines simplify and explain their observations. Together, these results point to underlying mechanisms reminiscent of satisficing in both people and machines, and illustrate how BCSS offers a general approach for interpreting and comparing rule-based reasoning of humans and black-box AI systems.

sections.body: Each ARC task gives two to five input-output grid pairs that share a hidden rule, and the solver builds an output for a test input. For one response at a time, the method starts from a reference program $P^{*}_{i}$ for the target rule and asks a large language model for $k$ independent sets of at most $j$ line edits. Each edited program is executed and kept only if it reproduces the response the model was conditioned on, so execution is the hard check and the model only proposes candidates. The programs are written in a symbolic domain-specific language. The section notes that the result is a set of final programs, not a process-level account of how the rule was inferred.
sections.heading: Behavior-Conditioned Symbolic Synthesis
sections.headline: Behavior-Conditioned Symbolic Synthesis searches for programs reproducing each individual response to abstract reasoning tasks, verified by execution.

sections.body: The study uses H-ARC, responses from over 1,700 participants to 800 public ARC-AGI-1 tasks. After filtering, the data contain 6,261 unique incorrect outputs across 723 tasks and 1,387 participants. Synthesized programs account for 49.1% of non-trivial incorrect attempts (3,636/7,402 pooled), with 52.5% on the training split and 46.2% on the evaluation split. Programs lie M=2.84 line edits from the reference on average (SD=2.04), and a median of 2 distinct programs explain each error. An exhaustive search over more than 16M single-line edits explains 25.8% of erroneous attempts. With 15 samples per response, BCSS recovers 89% of the exhaustively found matches. The section notes that exhaustive search becomes intractable at the edit distances where many errors lie. Estimates come from hierarchical Bayesian regressions reported with 94% highest-density intervals.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: Synthesized programs match 49.1% of non-trivial incorrect human attempts, against 25.8% for exhaustive single-edit search.

sections.body: The discussion reads three human regularities as consistent with satisficing. Programs explaining errors are shorter than the target rule beyond the procedure's own shortening, many errors fit some but not all training examples, and attribute misselection is the most common error type. Reasoning models show the same broad signatures, graded by resources. In GPT-OSS-120B, lower reasoning effort gives simpler programs and fewer partial fits. People and models fail on largely different tasks, which the authors take to suggest differing inductive biases. Stated limits: BCSS captures about half of non-trivial errors, the DSL was designed for solving ARC rather than for cognitive modeling, the proposing and classifying LLMs come from one model family, and the pipeline does not model how an agent arrived at a rule.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Human and model errors both show simpler, partial rules, consistent with satisficing under limited search.

sections.body: Filtering removes near-misses with up to two mismatched cells on grids of ten or more cells, copies of the test input, and empty 3×3 grids. Together these remove 15.6% (1,222/7,809) of unique incorrect grids. The DSL has 160 primitive functions and was released with 400 human-written reference programs for training tasks. For 361 of 392 evaluation tasks with errors, an LLM generated reference programs from five retrieved solved examples, and the remaining 31 tasks are excluded. For each unique error, the synthesizer samples 5 edit sets at each budget of 2, 4 and 8 lines, giving 15 samples. Sampling uses temperature 1.0, with Gemini 3 Pro on the training split and Gemini 3.5 Flash on the evaluation split. Each program is rewritten to remove causally irrelevant code, executed, and accepted only if it matches the error within the same tolerance.
sections.heading: Methods
sections.headline: Methods drop near-miss responses, synthesize missing reference programs, and sample 15 edits per error.

sections.body: This supplement covers four items: the noise-tolerance criterion behind the near-miss filter (§S1), per-split versions of the pooled human results (§S2 to §S4), per-model values for the human-versus-machine comparison (§S5), and the prompts used at each stage of BCSS (§S6).
sections.heading: Supplementary Information
sections.headline: The supplement reports the noise-tolerance rationale, per-split results, per-model machine comparisons, and all prompts.

sections.body: The section defends the near-miss filter. Incorrect responses of ten or more cells count as approximately correct if they differ from the correct test output in at most two cells. Supplementary Figure S1 shows representative responses within that interval, where grids differ in one or two isolated cells. Supplementary Figure S2 shows coverage at the cutoff, 52.5% for training and 46.2% for evaluation. The coverage curve keeps rising beyond the cutoff, so the threshold is described as conservative. The share of mismatched cells that are scattered singletons falls from about 60% at d=2 to about 35% by d=4. The authors state that residuals of three or more cells likely represent objects, but that more analyses are needed to confirm this. Table S1 reports trivial-error counts by split.
sections.heading: Filtering policy
sections.headline: A two-cell tolerance separates procedural noise from rule divergence, covering 52.5% of training and 46.2% of evaluation attempts.

sections.body: Table S2 splits the pooled coverage by reference-program source. Training references are hand-written and were sampled with Gemini 3 Pro. Evaluation references are model-synthesized and were sampled with Gemini 3.5 Flash. On training, 1,274 errors (47.3%) are reproduced, against 1,507 (42.3%) on evaluation. Exact-match coverage is 39.9% on training and 35.5% on evaluation. Program samples total 40,365 and 53,490. The median programs per error is 2 [1, 4] on training and 3 [1, 4] on evaluation. Mean effective edits per program are 3.30 on training and 3.63 on evaluation. The table reports yields only and does not separate the effect of the reference source from that of the proposal model.
sections.heading: Modeling coverage and program yield by split
sections.headline: Hand-written training references reproduce 47.3% of errors, versus 42.3% for model-synthesized evaluation references.

sections.body: Table S3 reports rule-type and order-effect estimates by split, attempt-weighted from the hierarchical categorical model. Programs consistent with at least one training example are 23.8% on training and 21.3% on evaluation. Partial matches are 22.1% and 19.7%, and alternative rules are 1.8% and 1.6%. Conditional on a partial match, the first-k prefix run is 41.0% on training and 30.1% on evaluation. The structured subset is 62.5% on training and 48.5% on evaluation. Values are posterior medians with 94% HDIs. The section reports these split differences as estimates without a separate test of the difference.
sections.heading: Rule types and order effects by split
sections.headline: Partial matches make up 22.1% of training and 19.7% of evaluation attempts, with 62.5% of training partial matches structured.

sections.body: Program length is regressed on reference-program line count and task success rate, with a term for error category. The grand-mean shortening is 9.2% (94% HDI [7.6,10.8]), and the seven cognitive categories span roughly 34 percentage points. Partial-program errors give programs 32.3% shorter than the target rule (94% HDI [29.1,35.6]). Boundary precision errors are predicted 2.0% longer than the reference, with an interval that includes zero (94% HDI [-3.0,7.3]). The authors read this ordering as showing that localized errors keep much of the target structure, while partial execution or wrong transformation selection yields coarser, shorter rules. The category estimates are interpreted as deviations from the grand mean.
sections.heading: Program length, reference complexity and error categories
sections.headline: Partial-program errors are 32.3% shorter than the target rule, while boundary precision errors show no reliable simplification.

sections.body: The section compares reasoning-model errors with human errors on 56 shared tasks, using classifiers trained on linearized program-level features. A classifier separating human from pooled model errors reaches within-task ROC-AUC of 0.65 to 0.69 across the three classifiers. Classifiers for GPT-OSS-120B at medium and low effort reach 0.68 to 0.77, with all 95% CI lower bounds at or above 0.59. For the more accurate configurations, discrimination is weaker and not reliably above chance, at 0.58 to 0.61 for Qwen3.5-27B and 0.57 to 0.63 for GPT-OSS-120B at high effort. The authors say the signal is spread across many weak cues rather than a few diagnostic operations.
sections.heading: Machine errors
sections.headline: Reasoning model errors share human error categories, but classifiers separate less accurate models from people more reliably.

sections.body: The section reproduces the pipeline prompt templates, with placeholders filled at run time. The error-program prompt gives the full DSL specification, the task grids, the reference program and the incorrect output grid, and asks for line edits under a fixed JSON schema. The reference-program prompt is retrieval-augmented with five solved training tasks and their human-written solvers, and is used for evaluation-split tasks that lack a hand-written solver. The error-classification prompt compares the reference program, the synthesized program and their behavior on training examples. It returns one of seven cognitive categories or the unclassifiable catch-all. The evaluation prompt shows the training pairs and asks the model to complete the held-out pair.
sections.heading: Prompts
sections.headline: Prompts for error-program synthesis, reference synthesis, error classification and machine evaluation are shown in supplementary figures.
